title: The Arecibo message
hook: A 1974 radio message to the stars was 1,679 bits long, a number chosen as a clue.
peek: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a short message towards a distant star cluster. Its length, 1,679 bits, was a deliberate hint: it can only be split into 23 rows of 73, or 73 rows of 23, and one of those makes a picture.
lede: On 16 November 1974, the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico celebrated an upgrade by sending a radio message into space. Frank Drake designed it, with help from Carl Sagan and others. It was a string of 1,679 on and off pulses. That number was a puzzle in itself: 1,679 is 23 times 73, and those two primes are its only factors.

bullets.text: A receiver curious enough to try the only possible rectangles would find that 73 rows of 23 columns produce a simple picture. The other way round gives nonsense, which is itself a clue.
The image includes the numbers one to ten, the elements that make up DNA, a sketch of its double helix, a human figure, our solar system with Earth singled out, and the Arecibo dish itself.
The message was beamed at M13, a cluster of several hundred thousand stars more than 20,000 light years away. It will take about that long to arrive, and the stars will have moved by then.
Drake and his team never expected a reply. The broadcast, which lasted about three minutes, was mainly a demonstration of what the newly upgraded telescope could do.
